problemSolved: Agents default to writing new code first and reaching for a dependency second, instead of checking whether the problem is already solved at a cheaper layer (existing code, stdlib, native platform feature).
mechanism: A strict-order checklist the model runs before writing anything: (1) does this need to exist at all — YAGNI, (2) already in this codebase — reuse, (3) stdlib, (4) native platform feature, (5) already-installed dependency, (6) can it be one line, (7) only then minimum new code. Explicitly framed as 'stop at the first rung that holds,' and explicitly NOT a substitute for reading the code first ('the ladder is a reflex ... but it runs after you understand the problem, not instead of it,' SKILL.md:44-48).
whyItWorks: It is pure prose reasoning scaffolding, not a lookup table the model executes mechanically — the model still has to recognize which rung applies to its specific case. This is the same class of mechanism as frontend-design's persona framing: it changes what the model checks for before generating, not what it is allowed to generate.
requiredContext: the existing codebase (rung 2 requires actually looking)
outputImpact: Measured, not asserted: agentic benchmark shows -54% mean LOC across 12 feature tasks vs a real Claude Code baseline with no skill, up to -94% on tasks with a native-platform substitute (date picker), ~0% on already-minimal backend CRUD (benchmarks/results/2026-06-18-agentic.md, lines 77-101).
failureModes: A model that treats the ladder as optional under time pressure and skips straight to writing code (no enforcement beyond the prose itself, since this is a prompt not a gate)
Rung 2 ("reuse what's already here") requires the model to actually search the codebase; a model that skips the search silently reinvents rather than reuses.
conflicts: None internal. External: a mechanical decision-tree implementation of the same ladder (a script that classifies rungs) would violate the C-no-mechanical-creativity constraint SiteSmith is rebuilding around — this must stay prose, never become code.
testMethod: Measured via the agentic benchmark (real Claude Code sessions, git-diff LOC, n=4 per cell), not a unit test — the mechanism's effect is on model behavior, which the repo tests by running real sessions and diffing output, not by asserting on the skill file itself.
sitesmithForm: Add an equivalent short reasoning ladder to SiteSmith's own build phase, ordered: does this need custom code at all → existing project pattern → framework/stack native feature → minimum new code. Keep it prose-only, never convert to a routing script.

problemSolved: A blanket 'write less code' instruction is dangerous on its own — it will cut input validation, error handling, and accessibility along with genuine bloat, because a model optimizing for brevity cannot tell the difference unprompted.
mechanism: A named exception list stated in the same file as the simplicity ladder: never simplify away input validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, or anything explicitly requested; plus a specific carve-out for physical/hardware calibration ('a real clock drifts ... leave the calibration knob').
whyItWorks: Puts the exception in the model's context at the same time as the instruction it limits, rather than trusting the model to independently infer where laziness should stop. This is the mechanism that keeps 'lazy' from degrading into 'careless.'
requiredContext: none beyond the skill text itself
outputImpact: Measured directly: on the agentic benchmark's adversarial safety tier, ponytail stayed 100% safe (20/20) while a bare 'YAGNI + prefer one-liners' prompt without this carve-out dropped a path-traversal guard once in 20 runs (benchmarks/results/2026-06-18-agentic.md:130-147).
failureModes: The carve-out list is finite and named; a trust-boundary category not on the list (e.g. rate-limiting against abuse, which is not explicitly named) has no equivalent protection.
testMethod: Measured via the same agentic benchmark's adversarial-input safety tier (deterministic exploit scripts run against the produced function) — a real execution test, not an assertion.
sitesmithForm: Pair any simplicity/YAGNI instruction in SiteSmith with an explicit, named list of what never gets cut for brevity: accessibility (contrast, alt text, keyboard nav), responsive layout correctness, and semantic HTML — stated in the same breath as the simplicity instruction, not in a separate section a model might not reach.

problemSolved: A deliberate simplification (accepted tradeoff, known ceiling) is indistinguishable from an accidental gap once the code is committed — 'later' silently becomes 'never,' and nobody can find or audit what was deferred.
mechanism: Every deliberate corner-cut gets a mandatory `ponytail: <ceiling>, <upgrade path>` comment naming the limit and the trigger to revisit it. `ponytail-debt` (skills/ponytail-debt/SKILL.md:16-38) then greps the whole repo for the marker and produces a ledger, flagging any marker with no named trigger as `no-trigger` rot risk.
whyItWorks: Converts an invisible mental note ('this is good enough for now') into a grep-able artifact. The marker plus the harvesting skill form a closed loop: mark → later, list → later, decide. Nothing here needs the model to remember anything across sessions; the ledger is regenerated from source each time.
outputImpact: Not separately measured; it is a bookkeeping mechanism, not a code-shape one. Its value is auditability, not LOC or correctness.
failureModes: Convention has no enforcement — a model can cut a corner and simply not leave the comment; nothing detects an *unmarked* shortcut, only unmarks the marked ones.
The `no-trigger` tag flags rot only for markers that exist; it cannot flag silently-undocumented debt.
testMethod: None automated in this repo beyond `grep -rnE '(#|//) ?ponytail:' .` itself, which is deterministic and testable but not tested here.
sitesmithForm: Give SiteSmith an equivalent marker for deliberate design/scope shortcuts taken during a build (e.g. a component intentionally left non-responsive below a breakpoint, a placeholder image), with a matching one-shot harvesting step so shortcuts are visible before a build is called done.

problemSolved: A minimized implementation with zero tests looks done but is unverified; 'lazy' can quietly mean 'unverified' instead of 'minimal.'
mechanism: Non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, a money/security path) must leave exactly ONE runnable check behind: an assert-based demo/`__main__` self-check or one small test file. Explicitly: 'No frameworks, no fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no test.'
whyItWorks: Sets a floor (something must be runnable and must fail if the logic breaks) without licensing the opposite over-build failure (a full test framework/fixture suite for a one-off script). It is proportional to the ladder philosophy applied to testing itself.
outputImpact: Not separately isolated in the benchmark; folded into the general safety-carveout results above (ponytail's discipline did not sacrifice the safety-tier pass rate).
failureModes: 'ONE runnable check' is a floor, not a coverage guarantee — a single assert can still miss most failure modes of non-trivial logic.
testMethod: Not separately tested; the mandate is prose the model follows, verified only by the correctness gate on the code it produces.
sitesmithForm: Apply the same floor to SiteSmith's build output: any non-trivial interactive component (form validation, a stateful widget) leaves one runnable check (a smoke test or manual verification step in verify.mjs), never a full test framework for a static marketing page.

problemSolved: Over-engineering (unlike correctness) has no deterministic check — but an unvalidated LLM judge is not evidence, it is an opinion with a confidence interval nobody has measured.
mechanism: A fixed judge model (claude-sonnet-4-6) at temperature 0 scores 0-3 against a published rubric, and must name the specific unnecessary construct or say 'none.' Before judging any real submission, `--selftest` requires the judge to rank a deliberately over-engineered reference strictly above a minimal reference for the same task (a hand-written `ComputeCache` with configurable TTL/LRU/stats vs. a one-line cache); if it fails to separate them, the run refuses to proceed ('judge not trustworthy; refusing to judge the matrix', judge.py:180).
whyItWorks: Turns an unfalsifiable 'the judge said so' into a gated claim: the judge's own discriminating power is checked with known-good/known-bad reference pairs before it is trusted on unknowns. This is directly transferable to SiteSmith's hardest problem (judging visual distinctiveness/over-genericness), which likewise has no deterministic check.
requiredContext: the reference over-built/minimal code pairs to selftest against
outputImpact: Used to produce the over-engineering-by-arm table in the agentic benchmark results; without the selftest gate this table would be unverifiable.
failureModes: Selftest reference pairs are hand-written by the same team running the benchmark — a judge could be tuned (deliberately or not) to pass exactly those two pairs while still being unreliable on real, more ambiguous cases.
Judge model itself could drift version-to-version without the selftest being re-run before every batch (the code re-runs it before `--run`, mitigating this, judge.py:179-180).
testMethod: `python judge.py --selftest` is itself the test: a pass/fail gate on whether the judge separates two known-different-quality references before being trusted on real data.
sitesmithForm: Build a self-validating LLM judge for SiteSmith's house-style/genericness problem: before judging any real build, it must first rank a deliberately templated/generic reference site below a deliberately distinctive one on the same brief, or the run refuses to score.

problemSolved: A lines-of-code metric alone rewards a broken one-liner exactly as much as a correct one; 'less code' is worthless without proof the code still works.
mechanism: Per-task harnesses actually execute generated code (spawns python/node) for tasks where that is tractable (email validator, debounce, CSV sum), appending real assertions and reading pass/fail from the exit code; falls back to structural/keyword regex checks only for tasks that cannot run headless (React component, FastAPI endpoint) with those cases explicitly documented as weaker (README.md, benchmarks/README.md:98).
whyItWorks: Pairs the measurement metric (LOC) with a hard correctness gate so the two can't be reported without each other — a benchmark that only measures brevity is gameable, one that also gates on real execution isn't.
requiredContext: per-task test harness code (hand-written per task, not generic)
outputImpact: Underwrites every LOC-reduction claim in the repo's README and benchmark tables — without it, the headline numbers would be unverified.
failureModes: Two of five task checks (React countdown, FastAPI rate-limit) are structural/keyword-only, not real execution — the repo is honest about this limitation but it does mean 40% of the harness doesn't actually prove correctness.
Per-task harness is hand-written and task-specific; doesn't generalize to new task types without new harness code.
testMethod: This *is* the test — a promptfoo assertion module wired into `benchmarks/promptfooconfig.yaml`, run against real model completions.
sitesmithForm: SiteSmith's own `scripts/verify.mjs` is already this pattern (screenshots, axe, console errors, dead links) for build correctness; extend the same execution-over-assertion principle to any future house-style/quality benchmark rather than trusting an LLM judge alone.

problemSolved: A flattering benchmark number, once published, tends to survive even after being shown to be inflated by a methodology flaw — most projects quietly keep citing the bigger number.
mechanism: The repo publishes its original single-shot number (80-94% less code), then documents a named critique (GitHub issue #126) that the baseline was a chatty bare model padding its answer with prose, rebuilds the benchmark as real Claude Code agent sessions on a real public repo instead, and reports the corrected, smaller number (-54% mean, near-0% on already-minimal code) alongside the original with the correction explicitly labeled 'the honest number.' It also documents catching its own measurement bug mid-project (a SessionStart hook silently firing on the baseline arm too, contaminating the comparison) and how it was fixed (per-arm process isolation, results:40-47).
whyItWorks: This is a methodology discipline, not a code mechanism — it is the same posture SiteSmith needs after its own 630k-token package lost 40-59 to a 55-line file: publish the uncomfortable number, name why the old one was wrong, and keep both visible rather than deleting the embarrassing result.
requiredContext: none — this is a documentation practice, not runtime context
outputImpact: Changes what claim can be defended: from 'ponytail cuts 80-94%' (overstated) to 'ponytail cuts 60-94% where there's an over-build trap, ~0% where there isn't, never drops a safety guard' (defensible, and the repo says so explicitly).
failureModes: Only as good as the next critique — nothing in the repo automatically re-audits the benchmark when a new critique arrives; the correction was manual and issue-driven, not self-triggering.
conflicts: This is exactly the discipline the two measured SiteSmith facts already demand — no conflict, but it is a process to adopt, not a line of code to port.
testMethod: The correction is itself methodological: isolate baseline from skill (`--setting-sources project,local`, `--plugin-dir` per arm), re-run against a real agent instead of a bare model, and publish per-task tables so the aggregate can't hide outliers.
sitesmithForm: When SiteSmith publishes any future benchmark, follow this same pattern: keep prior numbers visible, name the flaw a critic (or self-review) found, and report the corrected number as the number that counts — never quietly replace or delete the earlier claim.

problemSolved: Rung 4 of the ladder ('native platform feature covers it') requires the model to actually know dozens of native-vs-library equivalents across HTML, CSS, JS, Swift, Node, Python, and SQL — knowledge a model may not reliably recall under time pressure.
mechanism: A static markdown reference table mapping 'you think you need X library' to 'the platform already has Y' across seven domains (HTML elements, CSS, browser APIs, SwiftUI, Node stdlib, Python stdlib, database features), ending with an explicit escape hatch: 'when the native solution is genuinely insufficient ... the library earns its place. Install it then, not before.'
whyItWorks: This is a lookup table, but a load-bearing distinction applies: it is consulted by the model as reference knowledge to reason with, not executed as a decision script that picks the answer for the model. The model still has to recognize which row applies and judge whether the escape hatch fires.
requiredContext: only loaded when rung 4 of the ladder is reached — not needed every turn
outputImpact: Directly explains the benchmark's biggest wins (date picker -94%, color picker -92%) — the model reaching for `<input type="date">` instead of a library is this table's effect in practice.
failureModes: Frozen snapshot risk, same as any curated list: platform APIs gain new native features over time (e.g. `<dialog>`, `Object.groupBy`) and the table needs periodic refresh or it starts recommending yesterday's workarounds instead of today's native feature.
SwiftUI/Node/Python sections are irrelevant to a web-only skill and would be dead weight if copied wholesale.
testMethod: None automated — this is reference prose, not a tested artifact.
sitesmithForm: Build a much smaller, web-only equivalent (native HTML/CSS/browser-API table only, dropping Swift/Node-stdlib/Python/database sections entirely) as a progressively-loaded reference SiteSmith's build phase consults only when reaching for a component library, not as always-on context.

problemSolved: A single 'be simple' instruction conflates two different jobs: catching over-engineering while writing new code (in-the-moment) vs. finding what's already over-built in a repo (retrospective) — mixing them produces a vague tool that does neither well.
mechanism: Two narrowly-scoped one-shot skills sharing one tagging vocabulary (`delete:`/`stdlib:`/`native:`/`yagni:`/`shrink:`) but different scope: `-review` scans a diff, `-audit` scans the whole tree; both explicitly declare correctness/security/performance out of scope and route them elsewhere, and both end with a single quantified line (`net: -N lines`) rather than a narrative report.
whyItWorks: Narrow, single-purpose skills with an explicit non-goal statement ('Correctness bugs, security holes, and performance are explicitly out of scope') are easier for a model to execute correctly than one skill trying to do everything, and easier for a user to trust ('this only checks bloat, nothing else').
requiredContext: the diff (for -review) or the whole repo tree (for -audit)
outputImpact: Not separately benchmarked; this is a UX/scoping decision rather than a code-shape one.
failureModes: Two skills sharing a tag vocabulary must be kept in sync manually if the vocabulary changes (no shared source file between the two SKILL.md bodies, so drift is possible).
testMethod: None automated beyond the general test suite exercising skill file presence/structure.
sitesmithForm: If SiteSmith adds a post-build audit step, scope it narrowly (e.g. 'house-style/genericness audit only, not accessibility, not correctness') with its own single quantified output line, rather than folding it into a general review pass.

sourcePath: README.md:108-271 (Install section); 13 adapter directories at repo root
problemSolved: Getting the same ruleset in front of ~20 different agent hosts (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Kiro, Qoder, Gemini/Antigravity, Hermes, Devin, OpenCode, Pi, Swival, CodeWhale, Amp, Jules, Junie, OpenClaw) each with a different plugin/rule-file convention.
mechanism: 13 near-duplicate copies of the same ruleset text (`.cursor/rules/ponytail.mdc`, `.windsurf/rules/ponytail.md`, `.clinerules/ponytail.md`, `.kiro/steering/ponytail.md`, `.qoder/rules/ponytail.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `AGENTS.md`, plus plugin manifests for Claude/Codex/Devin/Qoder/Gemini/OpenClaw), synchronized only by a CI script (`scripts/check-rule-copies.js`) that byte-compares the compact copies against `AGENTS.md` and substring-checks 8 'invariant' phrases survive in both `AGENTS.md` and the longer `SKILL.md`.
whyItWorks: It works for a general-purpose coding-discipline skill distributed as an open-source project targeting every agent host in existence. It does not address a website-building problem at all.
outputImpact: Zero impact on SiteSmith's actual output quality — this is 100% distribution plumbing, not reasoning content. It is the part of ponytail's own repo that most resembles SiteSmith's own over-built 630k-token package: real complexity, but complexity spent on portability, not on the thing users evaluate.
failureModes: Byte-for-byte duplication across ~10 files is exactly the kind of surface a drift-detector is needed for at all — the mechanism it is protecting against (13 divergent copies of the truth) is self-inflicted by the choice to support this many hosts.
A canary-substring check (8 invariant phrases) is cheaper than full equality but by construction can miss any drift that doesn't touch one of the 8 chosen phrases.
conflicts: Directly conflicts with the proportionality principle this autopsy is judging against: SiteSmith targets one platform (Claude Skills); replicating this 13-host adapter surface would be reintroducing exactly the kind of unrequested scope that caused the original over-build.
testMethod: `node scripts/check-rule-copies.js`: byte-equality on 7 files after per-host frontmatter stripping, plus substring presence of 8 named invariant phrases in the two canonical sources.
sitesmithForm: N/A — SiteSmith ships as a single Claude Skill; do not add per-platform adapter directories or a drift-checker for platforms SiteSmith doesn't target. If SiteSmith ever needs cross-tool distribution, the underlying drift-check *technique* (canary substrings on load-bearing phrases) is reusable, but the 13-copy structure it protects is not.

problemSolved: If `skills/ponytail/SKILL.md` is missing or unreadable at runtime (e.g. a broken install), the hook needs something to inject instead of crashing silently.
mechanism: `getFallbackInstructions(mode)` hardcodes a ~30-line prose paraphrase of the same ladder/rules/carve-outs already written in `SKILL.md`, used only in the `catch` branch of `getPonytailInstructions` (line 89) when the real file can't be read.
whyItWorks: It works as a defensive fallback, but it is a second, hand-maintained copy of the same reasoning content living inside a `.js` file instead of the `.md` file that is supposed to be the single source of truth — the exact 'two places to update, one will drift' problem `check-rule-copies.js` exists to catch for the *other* nine copies, except this one is not covered by that script.
requiredContext: only triggers on file-read failure — dead code in the common case
outputImpact: None in the normal path; only matters in a broken-install edge case, which is rare enough that the duplicate is easy to forget about.
failureModes: This exact copy is NOT checked by `check-rule-copies.js` (which only covers `AGENTS.md` + 7 rule files, not this JS fallback string) — it is free to drift from `SKILL.md` silently, undermining the very sync discipline the rest of the repo enforces.
conflicts: Contradicts the repo's own stated discipline (drift-checked copies) by having one uncovered copy.
testMethod: None found — no test asserts the fallback text matches SKILL.md's content or invariants.
sitesmithForm: If SiteSmith needs a defensive fallback for a missing reference file, fail loudly (log and use a one-line generic instruction) rather than hand-maintaining a second full copy of the reasoning content that no test protects.
